criterion_notes.c1: Fails Criterion 1. Rather than examining household or community drinking-water or sanitation service access, this paper is a methodological participatory-research study focused specifically on 'opening up' the Capacity component of the Water Poverty Index (WPI) into a Water Prosperity Index (WPI+), centering on agricultural canal irrigation management (Samrat Ashok Sagar Irrigation scheme WUA), women's micro-credit SHGs, education, health/wealth, and perceived problem-solving responsibilities. Items such as indoor hand pumps and toilets belong to the separate Access component, which is not analyzed in this paper and is explicitly deferred to Wilk and Jonsson (2013).
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 in isolation, but fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading. Under the plain literal wording ('legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor'), Section 3.1 examines local institutional capacity, NGO-supported Water Users Associations (WUAs) and Self-Help Groups (SHGs), corruption perceptions, and divergences between community members and district government officials regarding perceived responsibilities for water-related problems. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 clarification, however, Criterion 2 is NOT met because the study examines participatory index co-production and generic organizational/capacity-building support (largely around agricultural irrigation and micro-credit) rather than any rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community water or sanitation service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff/cost-recovery rules, discretion/accommodation, enforcement, or utility regulatory structure). Note that plain_criterion2_decision is still 'exclude' because the paper independently fails Criteria 1, 4, and 5.
criterion_notes.c3: Meets Criterion 3. Contains primary empirical fieldwork conducted between 2006 and 2009 in a rural community in Vidisha district, Madhya Pradesh, including 16 participatory workshops using Participatory Poverty Assessment (PPA) tools, approximately 40 informal interviews, participant observation, local Panchayat/household survey data, and district statistics.
criterion_notes.c4: Fails Criterion 4. Reports Capacity-component indicator scores for WPI versus WPI+ (Table 3: child mortality, durable/land ownership, healthcare adequacy, self-confidence, perceived responsibility divergence for problem solving, WUA/SHG membership, social capital, literacy, school enrolment, education adequacy) and qualitative reflections on co-production. It does not report or analyze an outcome measuring household or community water or sanitation service access, connection, availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion (Table 2 measures opinion divergence on who is responsible for solving problems rather than service access, Figure 1 is omitted/blank in the postprint with only an unquantified passing remark on aggregate Access/Use index direction, and brief qualitative remarks on WUA canal maintenance concern agricultural wheat irrigation).
criterion_notes.c5: Fails Criterion 5. Although the community population (~100 households, unit of analysis: community/village index and workshop groups) and participatory case-study design are identifiable, there is no identifiable governance exposure to domestic water/sanitation service-access outcome relationship; the study compares expert WPI versus co-produced WPI+ capacity indicators.
criterion_notes.c6: Meets Criterion 6. Full text is written in English.

evidence_quotes.quote: The overall aim of this paper is to open up the Water Poverty Index with a special focus on the capacity to manage water in a robust way. This is done through a process of participatory research and by transforming the Water Poverty Index into a Water Prosperity Index using a local community in Central India as example.
The remaining factors relate to other WPI components and are further discussed by Wilk and Jonsson, 2013.

This section explores the institutional capacity of the local community in terms of the emergence of local collective solutions to common problems and linkages between community-district government management institutions.

Between 2006 and 2009, four field trips were undertaken and altogether 16 workshops arranged. With the help of the NGO, 14 gender-separate participatory workshops (7 with women and 7 with men) were held, attracting participants from the WUA, which encompassed all landowners and the SHGs, to which the majority of Hamlet women belong.

Finally, certain WPI indicators were considered irrelevant as determining their capacity by community members and were therefore omitted from the WPI+ (e.g. ownership of durable items not being a relevant measure of financial prosperity as even the poorest community members own televisions and cellular phones. Important items are indoor hand pumps and toilets, which were already included in the access component).

raw_response.exposure: Participatory co-production of knowledge ('opening up' the Water Poverty Index into a community-defined Water Prosperity Index) and general community institutional/learning capacity (NGO-supported agricultural irrigation WUA and women's micro-credit SHGs, perceived community vs. district-government responsibilities); no rule-type mechanism governing domestic water or sanitation service access
raw_response.outcome: Capacity-component indicator scores comparing WPI and WPI+ (child mortality, durable/land ownership, healthcare and education adequacy, rural literacy, school enrolment, self-confidence, perceived problem-solving responsibility divergence, WUA and SHG membership, social capital) and qualitative reflections on participatory co-production; no household or community water or sanitation service-access outcome analyzed
raw_response.population_and_sample: Rural community (Village and Hamlet) of approximately 100 households in Vidisha district, Madhya Pradesh, India; 16 participatory workshops (14 gender-separate with WUA and SHG members, 2 mixed with local government officials), approximately 40 informal interviews with community members, NGO staff, and district officials, plus community/household surveys
raw_response.rationale: Exclude (E01 — Wrong topic). Jonsson and Wilk (2014) is a methodological and participatory-research study on co-producing the 'Capacity' component of a composite water index (transforming the Water Poverty Index into a Water Prosperity Index) in a rural community in Madhya Pradesh, India. First, it does not examine household or community water or sanitation service access (c1 = no): its empirical analysis focuses exclusively on general water-management capacity indicators (health/wealth, formal and NGO adult education, self-confidence, agricultural canal irrigation WUA and micro-credit SHG membership, and perceived responsibility alignment), while the separate Access component (containing indoor hand pumps and toilets) is explicitly left to another paper (Wilk and Jonsson, 2013). Second, although it touches on local institutional capacity under the plain wording of Criterion 2, it fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2 (c2 = no) because it examines participatory index construction and generic NGO/community organizational capacity rather than any legal, regulatory, or administrative rule-type mechanism directly governing water or sanitation service access. Third, it reports Capacity-component scores and opinion divergences on problem-solving responsibility rather than any water or sanitation service-access outcome (c4 = no). Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the study remains excluded because it fails Criteria 1, 4, and 5.
raw_response.study_design: Participatory qualitative and mixed-methods case study (participatory workshops, informal interviews, household surveys, and index comparison of WPI vs. WPI+)
